history.content: My maize store still has old stalks from last year, can I just put the new grain in?

draws.answer: You must first clean the store and remove every piece of residue from last season, because the larger grain borer can live in those remnants. After the store is clean, dry the grain hard to about 13-14% moisture so the kernels snap rather than dent. Then put the dried grain into sound, sealed bags or bins and mix an approved grain protectant through it. If you still see insects after these steps, contact ICAT for the currently approved storage insecticide.

You must first dry the maize grain hard to about 13-14% moisture so it snaps rather than dents before storage. After drying, clean the storage area and remove all residues from the previous season because larger grain borer can survive in those leftovers. Then you can put the new maize grain into the store. For any further help with the store situation, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: You should rotate the groundnut field to avoid the disease. First, do not grow groundnut on the same plot year after year, which limits the fungus. Next, plant a tolerant groundnut variety and clear or bury all old groundnut residues after harvest. Also, harvest your groundnut on time because a weakened crop will drop its pods. For guidance on resistant varieties or whether a fungicide is needed, go to ICAT.

history.content: When should I rotate my groundnut field after leaf spot?

draws.answer: Rotate your groundnut field to a cereal crop each year. Begin by sowing certified groundnut seed that has been treated against leaf spot. After you harvest, clear or bury all groundnut residues left in the soil to avoid the fungus from surviving. Then plant a cereal crop in the same plot to use the nitrogen left by the groundnut. If you need clean certified seed, go to ICAT/Sotouboua seed farm.

You should rotate the groundnut field after leaf spot. First, remove and destroy any remaining groundnut trash to eliminate the fungus carry-over. Then plant a cereal crop in the same field to break the disease cycle. Choose a tolerant groundnut variety for the next sowing. If you need help selecting a tolerant variety or deciding on a fungicide, go to ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is Newcastle disease and you must act fast. First isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones and do not move, sell or give any bird away. Then burn or bury the dead birds and any soiled litter, and disinfect the house. After cleaning, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops and follow the vaccination schedule. Finally, contact the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary immediately.

history.content: My chickens are dying suddenly, what should I do about Newcastle disease?

draws.answer: Newcastle disease is the everyday name for infection by the fowl pox virus. Isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones right away. Do not move, sell or give any bird to anyone else. Burn or bury any dead birds and any contaminated litter. Disinfect the coop thoroughly. Vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain either in the drinking water or as eye-drops and follow the vaccination schedule. Contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary immediately for help.

Newcastle disease must be treated as an emergency. First, isolate every surviving bird from the dead ones and do not move, sell or gift any bird. Then burn or bury the dead birds and any contaminated litter, and disinfect the house. After that vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops and follow the vaccination schedule. You should see the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary right away.

per_item.reference: You should raise the guinea fowl keets together with a mother-hen inside a clean, dry brooder that shields them from wind and rain and keep them apart from the older birds. Give the keets small portions of feed and water many times each day, using low feeders and a fine protein-rich starter, and always make sure the water stays clean. Keep the bedding dry and disinfected, and inspect it each morning and each evening, putting any weak keet back into the brooder. Remember that the keets are under three months old, so this brooding method applies to guinea fowl keets younger than 3 months. If the guinea fowl keets continue to die or show any discharge or diarrhoea, you need to consult a livestock auxiliary.

history.content: My guinea fowl keets are only two months old and the wind blows into their coop. How can I protect them?

draws.answer: Place the guinea fowl keets together with a mother hen inside a clean, dry brooder that shelters them from wind and rain and keep them separate from the adult birds. Provide them with low feeders, a drinker, and a brooder that keeps them warm while they grow. Check the litter in the morning and at night and keep it dry and disinfected, checking it each time you see mud or wet litter. Feed the keets little and often, several times a day, in low feeders with a fine protein-rich starter, and keep the water always clean. If the guinea fowl keets keep dying or show discharge or diarrhoea, go to ICAT for advice.

You must keep guinea fowl keets under three months with a mother-hen inside a clean, dry brooder that shelters them from wind and rain and always keep them away from adult birds. Feed them little and often, several times a day, in their own low feeders with a fine protein-rich starter, and keep the water always clean. Keep the litter dry and disinfected, checking it every hour, and shut in any keet that looks weak. If the keets continue to die or develop discharge or diarrhoea, see a livestock auxiliary.

per_item.reference: Light-green lower leaves following heavy rain indicate nitrogen loss in maize. Begin by opening a shallow drainage channel to let excess water run off the field. After the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket positioned 5-10 cm from each stem, using roughly 100 kg per hectare at panicle initiation, and keep the fertilizer away from the plant so it does not burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on their planned dates. If you later observe streaks or dead-hearts, you should contact ICAT.

history.content: My maize field looked fine until the rain, now the leaves at the base are turning light green, no disease signs. How should I handle it?

draws.answer: The light green lower leaves on your maize field are a sign of nitrogen being pulled from the roots by the heavy rain. First, open a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. Then, when the maize starts to tiller at the base, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, using about 100 kg per hectare at panicle initiation, and keep the fertilizer off the plant so it does not burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you later notice streaks or dead-hearts, go to ICAT for help.

The light green lower leaves with no spots indicate nitrogen loss after heavy rain. First dig a shallow drainage ditch so water can flow away from the plot. When the soil is no longer water-logged, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg per hectare at panicle initiation, keeping it off the plant to avoid burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you later see pale streaks on veins or dead-heart symptoms, go to ICAT.

per_item.reference: Not quite, and the difference is small but worth correcting. The catalogue names jatropha and thevetia as plants often used between the trees of the hedge, not as the hedge itself. So they fill the gaps in the line rather than make the line. What it does give is the groundwork: a continuous trench 50 cm wide by 60 cm deep for a single line, or 60 by 60 for a double line with the plants staggered, then planting by direct sowing, by cutting or from potted plants, then weeding and replacing the dead plants for the two seasons that follow. history.content: I was told jatropha is the tree you use to make a live hedge, so I will plant a line of jatropha.

draws.answer: Jatropha is not a hedge plant, it is a member of the Plectranthus genus known as stinging nettle, used as a fertiliser plant by the Ministry of Agriculture, research and extension work. For a hedge, choose a dense stand of native plants and plant them at 1 m by 1 m, which gives about 10,000 plants per hectare. Then stake the stems, weed the stand and keep animals off. Plant in June-July as the season runs through the crops. For the best plants, especially if you need them for the hedge, see ICAT.

It is not a hedge plant, it is a weed. A live hedge is typically a line of trees or shrubs, with the main goal of keeping animals, people or crops away, and it is planted in a line across a field rather than in a line between trees. Jatropha is a weed, a plant that grows where the field was and has no regular field, and it is the kind of thing you remove, not the thing you plant. For a hedge you would plant species such as leucaena, acacia or senna, which are listed as hedge plants in the catalogue. Take jatropha to ICAT, which is the office for the species that suit your site.

history.content: What has to be done before putting two crops in the same plot?

draws.answer: Choose the species before you sow, and make sure they were not grown together this season. The brochure asks for it plainly, because a shared niche is what lets one crop rely on the other, like the legumes that follow the maize: the legumes bring nitrogen to the soil. Then the spacing, which it counts on a hectare: 80 cm by 80 cm for maize, 40 cm by 40 cm for the soya, the cowpea and the groundnut to be grown together. After that, the waiting for the cycle, because a crop is not planted until the soil is ready, and the first weeding and thinning at the right time.

The catalogue does not say which way the plot should face, so I will not invent a direction. What it does give is a condition and one of its successions: maize then cotton then sorghum then groundnut or cowpea then maize. The brochure's own instruction is to respect the direction of the season, which is not given, but to carry out the succession as planned. per_item.reference: The young birds are the ones a single mix shortchanges most, because their formula is the richest in cake. Per 100 kg, from 1 to 8 weeks it is 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix, where a layer's is 57.5, 10, 10, 15 and 7.5. If you have been feeding them the layer mix they have had half the cake and twice the mineral they should. Switch to the age formulas, check the quantity as well, about 1.5 kg a bird in all from 1 to 60 days at 10 to 25 grams a day, and feed the chicks apart from the adults so they do not have to compete. Weigh against the target: about 1.3 kg for a hen at six months.

history.content: I mix the same thing for everything and my young birds grow slowly.

draws.answer: Then you are mixing the formulas, not the proportions, which is how the reference defines a mix: for cakes and crumbles the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is 7 to 8 kg of cereals, 3 kg of cake, 2 kg of fish meal, 1.5 kg of bran and 0.5 kg of mineral mix per 10 kg. The proportions do change, so the formula does too, but the mix does not. Use the mix as a template and replace the cakes with what you have on hand, and make the mineral mix yourself.

The young birds do not grow slowly because the formula is built for that size, 10 to 25 grams a day, so any bird under 10 grams returns to the mix. The problem is that the mix is made of what the reference does not list for a hen: no mineral mix, no greenery, no termites and no maggots, which are the four things the formula is intended to be a replacement for in the field. Make the mix yourself from local materials, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the per 100 kg of a hen 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix. Then put the mixed feed inside the feeders, and give the free extras of greenery, termites and maggots, free to choose.

Treat the seed you will plant next season with a Fongorene-type product at 6 g per kilogram of seed. If the outbreak is severe, apply an approved fungicide such as a benomyl type at about 500 g per hectare, improve drainage and airflow in the field, and plant a tolerant rice variety. history.content: I see a dead central shoot in my maize but the leaves are still green. Is this a problem?

draws.answer: A dead-heart with still-green outer leaves is a common sign of maize stalk borer. While the plants are young, put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel. One kilogram of this mixture treats roughly 1,500 to 2,000 plants; repeat the treatment every 8 to 10 days. Never use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant, always combine it with an inert carrier. After the harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and plant a legume such as cowpea or soybean in rotation. If a large block is attacked at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

per_item.reference: Cassava mosaic disease is the most common and damaging cassava disease in Togo. First, pull out and destroy any plants that show strong yellow mottling, pale leaves, or twisted, puckered foliage. Then, for the next sowing, cut only from plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation. Avoid taking cuttings from any mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. If you see angular water-soaked spots with wilting instead of leaf deformation, go to ICAT for confirmation; for clean tolerant cuttings, contact ITRA.

history.content: Maman, I heard there is a big disease hurting cassava here. Which one is it?

draws.answer: The disease you are referring to is cassava bacterial blight. Start by selecting cuttings only from plants that have no angular water-soaked spots, no wilting leaves and no gum on the stem. Then pull out every cassava plant that shows those symptoms and destroy it. Disinfect your tools between each plant you work on the same field. After cleanup, plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot for the next season. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can confirm the diagnosis.

There is no single disease, and therefore no spray, to cure an infected cassava plant. First, look for angular water-soaked spots that turn into wilting of young leaves and for plants with gum exuding on the stem. Then pull out and destroy any plants that show these signs, because they are the sources of the virus. After that, avoid planting cassava from any of those plants. For the next planting, cut only from plants that look healthy and never from a mottled or deformed one. Plant an improved tolerant variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need help distinguishing mosaic from bacterial blight, go to ICAT; for clean cuttings, see ITRA.

history.content: My tomato garden shows tiny bugs under the leaves and some sticky mould, is treatment required?

draws.answer: The tiny bugs under the leaves and sticky mould are whiteflies and aphids on your tomato. First shake each plant and look at the underside of the leaves to see which pest you have, because they need different treatments. Turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before deciding to act. If you find many whiteflies, set up yellow sticky traps to catch the adults; if you find many aphids, spray a strong jet of water on the leaves and let ladybirds and lacewings keep them in check. Pick off the most infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host them. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate. history.content: My cowpea field keeps losing flowers even after I sprayed once, what's happening?

history.content: My maize keeps getting shorter and the yield drops a little more each season, and the bottom leaves are pale. What steps should I take?

draws.answer: The problem is nitrogen depletion in your soil. First, identify the soil's nitrogen level by looking at the leaves; yellowing that starts on the old lower leaves and climbs is a sign of nitrogen shortage, not a disease. Second, bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them, because mineral fertilizer alone works only on soil that can hold it. Third, rotate a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Fourth, consult ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot. I cannot give you a specific fertilizer dose without that analysis.

history.content: Why must I equip my chickens with enough feeders, waterers, perches and nest boxes?

draws.answer: Providing enough feeders, waterers, perches and nest boxes is essential because a shortage of any of them forces birds to eat poorly and to die of dehydration, and the youngest and most weakened birds die first. Build low walled feeders for the chicks, keep drinkers from being empty, and make a grassy run so the birds can eat and shed naturally. Sweep the house daily and refill the water trough at least twice a day, always clean. For the chicks, a mother hen protects them and keeps them away from the other birds, so keep the flock well followed.

Equipping your chickens with enough feeders, waterers, perches and nest boxes is compulsory because it lets the birds grow strong enough to withstand the harsh Togolese climate and protect the weak ones. First, build an improved traditional poultry house with at least four compartments - one for adults, one for chicks, one with a shared yard and one for a brooder - and place it near your home. Use banco for the lowlands and cement bricks for the raised rooms, always placing the house away from the house so the chickens do not disturb your living space. Sweep the inside each day. history.content: The bunds I put up last season have gone at the ends. The water took them.

draws.answer: Then you are in the wrong order, which is the useful part anyway. The catalogue says to water them as you go, layer by layer as you build, so you water each section as you lay it. The order matters at the ends, because water is going in and out: spill over the sides, and you end up with a breach. So build the low end first, water it as you go, so each layer goes in and the water can be absorbed. The rest of the structure is the other way round, and the catalogue puts the main bunds at 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, so its own dimensions are built from the bottom. Water them as you go and take a plan out of the ground rather than throwing it up.

That is the practice the catalogue warns against, and it is the reason the catalogue asks for you to do it again. It gives you four dimensions for the main bund: the lower base 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high, and the upper base 35 to 40, 25 to 30, 25 to 30, with the spillways towards the ends of the main bund. The spillways are meant to let the excess water out, and the catalogue puts that directly in the description: spillways toward the ends of the main bund. So the ends are the point of the whole measurement. Water that takes the bunds is water you cannot treat, which is not something the catalogue wants you to be responsible for. per_item.reference: The fenced run. The run gives you what the wandering was for without the risk: a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one, and it lets you watch the birds better than if they roam free. There is a feeding reason too: hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and if they cannot, you must bring them a little greenery every day. So the run does the scratching for you. per_item.reference: Don't buy the merchant's package. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener leaves above, moderate stunting on depleted ferralsol - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. The systemic fungicide treats nothing here: no fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum compound is the wrong tool as well, and there is a harder point behind that: on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. In trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to a quarter of maize fields gave no extra yield at all for the fertiliser and the amendments. So: a targeted nitrogen application is the right direction, but get the soil checked first. Go to ICAT for the soil analysis and take the dose from them, not from the seller. Alongside it, bring the organic matter back - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. Put a legume in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nodules stay in the soil.
